$comment: The catalog of plugins cxagent knows about. One entry per plugin; the ones cxagent itself
releases also have a directory beside this file.
MACHINE-READABLE ON PURPOSE. The plugin picker reads this to show what is available and where
to get it, so it does not have to parse a README or hardcode a list. Keep it truthful by hand
until something generates it — an entry naming an asset no release carries is worse than no
entry at all. CatalogTests checks each entry against the plugin's own sidecar.
FIRST-PARTY AND THIRD-PARTY ENTRIES DIFFER IN ONE FIELD: `source`. A first-party plugin says
`{ "kind": "release", "asset": "..." }` and is fetched from cxagent's own release, pinned
to the version being installed. Anything else names where it actually lives, and the fields
below stop being a formality: nobody needs telling who wrote a plugin that ships in the same
zip as the binary, and everybody needs telling for one that does not.
WHAT THE HASH IS AND IS NOT. `sha256` is over the downloaded artifact, and proves the bytes
arrived unaltered. It says nothing about who wrote them — that is `publisher` and
`repository`, which are claims a reader judges, not facts a client can verify. The separate
hash the load prompt shows is over the INSTALLED load set, and answers a different question:
has anything changed since you approved it.
generated from the artifacts themselves. A plugin hosted elsewhere DOES carry `sha256` here,
The `$example` below is not installed and is not a real plugin. It is here so the third-party
shape has one worked instance to copy, and so a client parsing this file meets both `source`
HOW A CLIENT BUILDS THE DOWNLOAD URL. A `url` source is fetched as written. A `release` source
is NOT a fixed URL on purpose — it tracks whichever cxagent release is being installed, and a
URL written here would pin a version this file cannot know. `urlTemplate` says how to build one
from `repo`, `asset` and the tag the client is installing; `latest` is GitHub's own
always-current alias, for a reader who just wants the newest and has no tag in hand.
install.sh does not read this file — it is the bootstrap, and substitutes $TAG itself. The
template exists so every OTHER client agrees with it instead of hardcoding the same convention.
`sha256` ON A RELEASE ENTRY IS WRITTEN BY THE RELEASE, NOT BY HAND. The artifact does not exist
until the workflow builds it, so a hand-written hash would be a guess; a generated one is a
fact. The release computes it, commits it here with the tag it belongs to in `stampedAtTag`,
and a reader can tell a current hash from a stale one by comparing that tag to the version they
are installing. Null before the first release that carries the plugin.
`checksums` stays beside it: SHA256SUMS is generated from the artifacts themselves at release
time, so it is the authority. This field is the convenience — a client that has only this file
can check a download without fetching a second asset.

plugins.name: csharp-lsp
plugins.description: Go-to-definition, find-references and diagnostics for C#, backed by a language server. Crosses project boundaries: a reference in a test project resolves into the project under test.

requires.description: A C# language server on PATH. csharp-ls is the default and needs no configuration.

settings.server: The language server command. Defaults to csharp-ls.
settings.args: Arguments for it. OmniSharp needs ["-lsp"]; csharp-ls needs none.

$example.description: The same three operations for Rust, backed by rust-analyzer.
